html:
Three complete original text models

Story for a classmate — The missing note. Mila carried a note to the school garden. A breeze blew it under a bench. She asked Amir to help, and he found it beside a plant pot. Mila thanked him and put the note safely in her bag.

Information for a new classmate — Our model class library.

Where books go: Our class library has two shelves. Story books go on the upper shelf. Information books go on the lower shelf.

How to return them: Put a book back with its cover facing the front. This helps the next reader see its title.

Request to our teacher — A reading box. Please put a reading box beside the mat. We could choose books without crossing the room, and we could return them after quiet reading. A box there would help our class find a book. Could we try it this week?

These are invented teaching situations. Notice the story’s linked events, the information headings and the request with a relevant reason. Sort the planning cards below by their purpose, then explain a match.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Planning cards to sort and use

  • Card A: Reader: a classmate. Purpose: entertain. Plan: a paper hat blows away; a friend catches it; the owner puts it away safely. Write a linked story with an ending.
  • Card B: Reader: a new classmate. Purpose: inform. Supplied model facts: the art tray is by the window; clean pencils go in the blue pot; used scrap paper goes in the paper box. Group the facts under useful headings.
  • Card C: Reader: the teacher. Purpose: persuade. Request a quiet drawing corner. Give a relevant reason and a polite action to try.
Check the planning matches

A is imaginative story writing, B is informative writing and C is persuasive writing. Each requires an actual short written text. For C, accept different relevant reasons rather than one fixed opinion.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Sentences and word choices

Simple: The small seed tray was resting on the shelf.

Noun group: The small seed tray. The words work together to name and describe a thing. Whole verb group: was resting. Keep both words when identifying what was happening.

Compound: The soil was dry, so Mila added water. “The soil was dry” and “Mila added water” can each stand alone; so links the first situation to its result.

Contrast: Mila packed seeds and soil. And joins two things here, not two complete messages. A comma is not needed just because and appears.

Word bank: seed tray, soil, shelf, basket, garden, paper. Basket, garden and paper each have two syllables in the model’s ordinary pronunciation. Say the word, notice familiar sound–letter patterns and check its conventional spelling.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
An edit you can explain

Draft: “mila took a thing to the garden. She put it it on the shelf”

Intended meaning: Mila carries a seed tray. She puts it on the shelf in the garden.

Revised: “Mila took a seed tray to the garden. She put it on the shelf.”

  • Replace thing with seed tray so the reader knows the object.
  • Delete the repeated it; keep one it to refer to the seed tray.
  • Add the opening capital and final full stop.

Read it back: do the actions stay in a sensible order, and do the words still convey the intended meaning?
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Create and edit a simple digital text

With an adult, use a familiar drawing or document tool. Create two pages or panels: first Mila carries the seed tray; next she puts it on the shelf. Type a caption for each and draw a matching picture. Use these original starting captions: “Mila carries a seed tray.” and “She puts it on the shelf.”

  1. Create the two panels and captions.
  2. Check their order. If the shelf panel comes first, move it after the carrying panel.
  3. Replace an unclear word, such as thing, with seed tray; delete any repeated word and check capitals and full stops.
  4. Read the changed text with the adult. Check each picture matches its caption.
  5. Save locally with adult help. Share it only with the agreed familiar reader.

A paper drawing-and-caption version practises the same text choices. The digital elaboration requires actually making and revising a digital version; describing a button alone does not demonstrate it.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A fresh written check

Reader: a new classmate. Purpose: inform. Use these invented model facts: the craft tray is beside the door; clean brushes go in the red pot; paper scraps go in the paper box. Write a heading and a few linked sentences. Then explain one word choice or edit.

Check the writing and the earlier quick checks

The heading should fit craft storage; the text should accurately group the given facts so the reader can find the materials. Accept different clear sentences. Look for a precise topic word, sensible pronouns and simple punctuation. Earlier checks: plan purpose, reader and ideas before drafting; choose a structure that helps that purpose; a compound links two complete messages; check meaning and order before surface corrections.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Show what you can create

For a familiar classmate, write a new short story in which a paper hat blows away and someone helps recover it. Include linked events and an ending, then reread and improve one sentence. In another short session, write a polite request to the teacher for a quiet drawing corner, with a reason connected to the request. Judge the actual texts and the learner’s explained edits.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete original presentation and useful cue

For classmates: “Today I will explain how our reading box works. First, choose one book from the box. Next, return it with its cover facing the front. This helps the next reader find a book. Thank you for listening.”

Facts for this model: the box is beside the mat; it holds books for quiet reading; return each book with its cover facing the front.

Cue to make and use: draw three boxes, label them Choose, Read and Return, and connect them in that order. Point to the relevant box as you explain it. The cue shows the sequence; it does not stand in for speaking.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Rehearse, listen and improve

  1. Deliver the complete reading-box talk to a familiar listener, using your three-box cue.
  2. Ask “Where does the book go when you finish?” and “Was there a part you wanted me to explain again?”
  3. Listen to the actual response. Choose one change, such as pausing before the return step or making cover facing the front clearer.
  4. Practise and deliver the revised version. Ask whether the change helped.

Observer notes: Was the topic clear? Could the listener follow the order? Were the topic words useful? Was the message audible or accessible, with helpful pace and pauses? Record any modelling, prompting, script, AAC or other support used.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Two purposes; purposeful delivery

Welcome to a visiting class: “Welcome to our reading corner. I will show you how our reading box works.”

Care reminder: “Please put the books here. Keep their pages flat so the next reader can use them.”

An adult models each aloud in its stated situation. Then model the same words, “Please put the books here”, as a friendly invitation and a calm care reminder. The learner tries each and asks the listener which intention was clear.

Tone conveys intended attitude, volume supports hearing and pace controls the rate and pauses. Discuss actual listener feedback; no printed mark can specify a single correct pitch pattern for every voice.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A different presentation to prepare

Familiar audience: a classmate. Purpose: explain how to make a folded paper card. Materials: one piece of scrap paper; no scissors.

Given sequence: put the paper flat; bring one short edge to the other short edge; press along the fold; open the card to show the inside.

Prepare your own opening, explain the steps in order and finish by naming what you made. Make a cue with four numbered boxes or demonstrate with the paper. Rehearse, ask which step was least clear, improve it and deliver again.

What should a listener understand?

They should recognise the card-making goal and follow the supplied order. A useful ending names the folded card. Accept different clear wording and appropriate access modes. Observe actual delivery and the feedback-based change.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A fresh presentation check

Audience: your familiar class. Purpose: explain how a model art tray is organised. Supplied facts: clean pencils are in the blue pot; paper scraps are in the paper box; the tray is beside the window.

Prepare an opening, related points, a useful cue and an ending. Rehearse with a listener, ask a specific clarity question, change one feature and deliver the revised version.

Observer guidance and earlier quick checks

Check that the actual talk uses the facts accurately, has a useful order and uses words such as pencils, scraps and tray clearly. Listen for purposeful tone, accessible volume, pace and pauses in the chosen mode. Note the learner’s own contribution and any support. Earlier checks: rehearse to try and improve the talk; an opening names the topic or purpose; pace and pauses give thinking time; a visual helps when it explains or cues a relevant part.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A useful reflection

After the actual presentation, complete: “My listener understood ___. I changed ___ because ___. In the next attempt I will ___.” Use real feedback. The reflection supports assessment but does not replace the presentation.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Prepare a real handwriting model

Have suitable paper, a comfortable pencil or agreed adapted writing tool, and a nearby model in the learner’s school-taught unjoined script. An adult writes the target words slowly using that model, showing the actual starting points and movements. The learner watches, then writes beside it without tracing. The typed words here identify the targets only; they do not provide a stroke-order model.

Use the preferred writing hand. Adjust paper position and support the paper with the other hand if helpful. Look for comfortable control during writing, following individual school or specialist advice. Do not insist that every learner use one finger arrangement.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete handwriting targets

Case comparison: Mia and mia. The first can be a person’s name; the second is a case-comparison target. Watch the adult’s local-script capital M and lower-case m.

Word targets: Sam; bag; paper; garden. Watch each adult-written model and write it yourself with unjoined letters.

Sentence targets: Mia has a blue bag. / Sam has a red mug. / We put a bag here.

Copy one short target at a time beside the real model. Check the intended letter order, case, recognisable forms and word spaces. The task supplies the spellings so attention can stay on handwriting.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Check relative size and placement

An adult demonstrates a, b, g and B in the learner’s taught style on suitable lines. Compare the short body of a, the tall part of b and the part of g below the baseline. Capital B has a different form from lower-case b. Exact shapes follow the school model.

Then the adult writes “a big bag”. The learner copies it. Ask the adult to point to a readable short letter, a tall letter, a part below the baseline and the spaces between the three words. Keep letters within a word together, with clearer word gaps.

The baseline is a guide to placement. It does not mean forcing all parts of all letters above it. Use adapted guides if these support comfortable readable writing.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Compare actual attempts over time

Write the adult-modelled sentence “Mia has a blue bag.” Keep the dated sample. Circle one clear word and choose a target, such as the gap after has or the taught movement for b. Practise that feature briefly, then use it in the sentence.

In a later short session, repeat under similar conditions with the same useful model and tools. Compare recognisable forms, word gaps, hesitation, comfort and effort. An adult observes actual movement and grasp when these are being discussed. Better ease with readable words is more useful than rushing.

Note support and changed conditions. Two attempts made immediately after modelling show current practice; a series of comparable samples helps discuss growth. Stop if there is pain or strain.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A fresh actual handwriting check

The adult writes “Tom put a bag on the shelf.” in the learner’s taught unjoined script. The learner watches, then writes it beside the model without tracing. Check the actual words and, where relevant, observe their production. Circle one readable feature and name one improvement.

Observer guidance and earlier quick checks

Look for the supplied letter order and case, recognisable unjoined forms, useful relative size and clear spaces between words. Observe comfort and functional control rather than inferring a grasp from the finished page. Earlier checks: legible writing has recognisable shapes and clear word boundaries; spaces show the boundaries; letter bodies follow the baseline while some parts extend below it; fluency grows through short accurate practice and comparable evidence of increasing ease.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Make one useful next step

Choose a feature from your real writing, such as a clear capital, a word gap or a letter’s starting movement. Compare it with the nearby adult-written school model. Practise briefly and use it in another word. Check comfort and readability before trying to write more quickly.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete sound-card routine

Use counters or finger taps, not small loose objects with a learner who might put them in their mouth. The adult models fresh: /f/, /r/, the vowel in bed, /sh/. Four phonemes need four counters. The letters sh spell one sound; f and r in the cluster are separate sounds. Show fresh after the spoken model.

For a two-syllable model, say cloudy naturally and clap its two syllables. Then segment five phonemes with counters: /k/, /l/, the vowel in cloud, /d/, the final vowel in happy. Do not treat a whole syllable as one phoneme.

Adult oral-task card · keep the screen away from the learner

Say each word clearly and give only the spoken instruction. Do not read its answer first. 1. “Say slip without the first /s/.” 2. “Say best without /s/.” 3. “Say tent without the final /t/.” 4. “Say clap. Change the final /p/ to /m/.”

Check the oral tasks

1. Lip. 2. Bet, keeping final /t/. 3. Ten. 4. Clam. Observe what the learner actually says; reteach only the changed sound if needed. A supplied model counts as support.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Build, improve and explain a word chain

Adult models the spoken chain slam → slim → swim. First swap the vowel in cat for the vowel in sit. Next swap /l/ for /w/. All other sounds stay in order at each change. After the oral turns, show the print, write each word and reread it. Explain where the phoneme was changed.

For a fresh turn, the adult uses a different card from the formative check below with print covered. Reading this displayed chain is useful practice, but does not establish independent oral manipulation.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Quick-answer checks and fresh oral transfer

Check the earlier quick questions

A phoneme is a speech sound that can distinguish words. Frog has four phonemes: /f/, /r/, its vowel, /g/. Stop without /s/ is top. Changing the initial /m/ in map to /t/ gives tap.

Fresh adult oral card · keep print covered

Ask “Say plan without /l/.” Then ask “Say clap. Change its first /k/ to /f/.” Let the learner answer aloud before showing print. Ask them to write and reread each resulting word. For Stretch, say slam, change its vowel to the vowel in sit, then change /l/ to /w/, one step at a time.

Check the fresh responses

Plan without /l/ gives pan. Clap with initial /f/ gives flap. The two-step chain gives slim, then swim. Accept the learner’s consistent local sounds; written results are pan, flap and swim. Oral manipulation, written encoding and rereading each require their own observed response.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete reading and sorting cards

Read these cards: green, moon, book, rain, play, beach, bread, night, frog, crisp, knee, thumb, raincoat, sunset, rabbit. Point to the spelling that supports each reading. Sort by vowel pattern, consonant cluster, silent letter or compound. Some words can fit more than one group.

Check the sort and explain the overlaps

Examples: green has ee; moon and book have oo with different vowel sounds; rain has ai; play has ay; beach and bread have ea with different vowel sounds; night has igh for long i plus final /t/. Frog begins /f/ and /r/; crisp begins /k/ and /r/ and keeps /s/ and /p/ at the end. Knee has silent k; thumb has silent b. Raincoat and sunset are compounds. Rabbit has two syllables but is not built from two complete words.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Map, write and reread

Model rain as r | ai | n: three phonemes. Model thumb as th | u | mb: three phonemes in the usual pronunciation, with b not pronounced separately. Model robot by reading its two syllables and joining them. These are sound and spelling models, not three universal rules for every word.

Adult dictation card · hide all printed targets

Choose a word whose patterns the learner has been taught. Say “tail” in “The dog wagged its tail”; “bright” in “The lamp is bright”; or “sunhat” in “I packed my sunhat”. The learner says the word, maps its sounds, writes it and reads the spelling back. Say the target word and its sentence aloud. Keep the printed word hidden and do not name its letters or show its spelling until the learner has written it.

Check the writing

Tail uses ai; bright keeps the /b/ and /r/ cluster and igh for long i; sunhat combines sun and hat. Check the actual letters, not only whether the learner can select a printed answer.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Quick-answer checks and transfer

Check the earlier quick questions

Ai often spells the long a vowel as in rain. K is silent in knee. Sun and set form sunset. A grapheme is a letter or group of letters used to represent a phoneme.

For a fresh reading check, read bright and sunhat without an adult reading the target first. Explain the igh spelling and the two complete words sun and hat. Then use a covered adult dictation turn from the earlier packet to check actual writing and rereading.

Check the reading explanation

Bright keeps /b/ and /r/ as separate initial sounds and igh spells long i; final t remains /t/. Sunhat joins sun and hat. Knowing parts helps, but the learner must still read the complete word.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete word-analysis cards

Read said, friend, come and have. Point to the unusual part: ai in said and ie in friend spell the vowel in bed. Come and have show that final e does not always signal a long vowel. Read each whole word and its useful consonant clues.

Compare one, once, only and lone with an adult’s spoken model. One and once begin with a /w/ sound despite having no written w; only and lone have the long o vowel. Compare their exact spellings without treating them as a simple rule for adding one suffix to every word.

Check the model analysis

Map the useful sounds before marking the unexpected part. The same ai spelling can represent different vowels in rain and said; the same short vowel can be written differently in said and friend. Keep the known base friend when writing friendly.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete related-word and context tasks

Read these pairs: jump → jumped; play → played; want → wanted. Explain the past ending ed although its sound differs. Build help + ful, play + ed and jump + ing; use each in a sentence. Read “The wind shook the branch” and “Please wind the toy”, attending to the meaning and all the printed letters.

Check the word parts and reading

Helpful means giving help; played marks that the playing happened in the past; jumping names the ongoing action in “I am jumping.” The bases help, play and jump remain visible. Wind has the vowel in sit for moving air, and rhymes with find for turning the toy. Context selects a plausible reading; it does not replace the word with a synonym.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Quick answers and a covered spelling turn

Check the earlier quick questions

A high-frequency word occurs often. In said, ai unexpectedly spells the vowel in bed. A morpheme can preserve a useful base or ending, such as help in helpful or ed in jumped. Analysing known and unusual parts makes the exact spelling easier to learn than treating the entire word as an unexplained shape.

Known base card: paint. Read the base before starting the covered spelling turn.

Adult dictation card · learner looks away

Say “some” in “There is some milk”, relating its vowel spelling to the previously read come only if support is needed. Then say “painted” in “Yesterday I painted a box”. Hide the base and target models while the learner writes, then ask them to reread.

Check the writing and support used

Some uses o for the vowel heard in come, with a final e. Painted keeps paint and adds ed, which adds a syllable here. Check exact written forms some and painted; an analogy prompt is support and should be recorded.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete base and affix cards

Bases: play, help, kind, cover, friend. Prefixes: re, un. Suffixes: er, ful, ing, ed, ness, ly, ship. Make conventional words and explain them in a sentence; do not assume every card joins to every base.

Sort the affix cards by position: re and un go before a base; these suffix cards go after. Use the actual meaning of each finished word to check your choice.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Family boundary check

Compare play, replay, player and day. Replay and player contain the meaningful base play; day shares a rhyme, not that base. Compare kind, unkind and nice: nice can have a similar meaning, but does not contain kind.

Check and explain

A morphemic family needs a shared meaningful base, not just matching sounds or a similar meaning. A valid new word must also have a conventional spelling and fit the sentence in which it is used.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Quick answers and a new family

Check the earlier quick questions

A base is the meaningful part used to build the family. A prefix goes before it. Ful adds a quality in words such as helpful; it is spelled with one l. Valid play-family examples include player, played, playing and replay; explain their meanings, rather than accepting every letter combination.

New known base: pack. Read and write pack once, then cover it.

Fresh family task · answer after attempting

Write a word meaning pack again. Explain the prefix, use the new word in a sentence and reread it. Then build a word for someone who packs and explain which ending you added.

Check the family

Repack = re + pack, meaning pack again: “I will repack my bag.” Packer = pack + er, someone who packs: “The packer filled the box.” Both retain pack. Accept another conventional word only when it satisfies the precise meaning and uses the named base.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.
